column1: • Empathy: You acknowledged Betty’s emotional struggles (""Yes, it has to be difficult to handle that, especially when you are a caregiver""), and validated her feelings often (""that has to be difficult"", ""I think you are doing a very good job""). This demonstrated empathic listening consistent with MVP.

• Respect for Patient Values: You explicitly recognized the importance of honoring Jerry’s wishes and independence (""we have to respect him and his previous decision""), helping Betty feel supported in honoring his values.

• Explicit Information: You shared the seriousness of the situation clearly (""your dad...is going through a very difficult Pneumonia to treat and also a respiratory failure...there is a bad prognosis""), avoiding jargon for the most part. You explained DNR in simple terms.
• Reassurance of Support: Throughout, you reassured Betty of team support (""we are here to support you in all the process""), which fosters trust.
• Open Door for Questions: You encouraged questions at the end and expressed ongoing availability (""if you have any other question...just let me know"").

• Empower: Elicit Concerns Early and More Clearly: You could strengthen empowerment by starting with an open-ended question about Betty’s understanding and concerns (""Can you tell me what you understand about your dad's current situation?""). This ensures her agenda is addressed early.

• Empower: Ask Permission & Teach-Back: Before sharing prognosis, ask for permission (""Would it be okay if I shared what we’re seeing?""). After giving information, use teach-back (""Can you tell me in your own words what you understand about what we discussed?"") to gauge her understanding.

• Be Explicit: Clarify Trajectory & Options Further: Consider being more precise about Jerry’s expected clinical trajectory and the purpose/limits of intubation – e.g., ""Even if we use a breathing machine, he is very unlikely to regain the independence he values."" Explain comfort-focused care as a positive, proactive choice, not merely what’s left when everything else fails.

• Empathize: Pause for Emotion: When Betty expressed her inner conflict (""I want him to fight but also don't want to push him into something he’s against""), pause, name the emotion, and validate it (""It sounds like you’re torn between wanting to do everything for him and respecting his wishes – that’s an incredibly hard, loving position""). Allowing for silence can deepen empathy.

• Language & Clarity: The phrase ""we used to give him a DNR"" is awkward/confusing. Say, ""We would recommend a DNR order to align with his wishes, which means we won’t use CPR or breathing machines if his heart or breathing stops.""

• Facilitate Family Planning: Offer guidance about how and when Betty might share this information with other family, aligning with MVP’s empowerment (“Would you like support when talking to other family members about the plan?”).
• Open conversations by eliciting the surrogate’s understanding and priorities before diving into medical details.
• Name emotions and pause intentionally to process difficult news.
• Frame comfort-focused care/DNR as active, patient-centered decisions rather than just avoiding intervention.

column1: • Listening: You gave the patient space to share their concerns about work, parenting, and anxiety. This showed some effort to empower the patient to express their feelings and situation.
• Follow-up Planning: You offered to continue the discussion tomorrow. This can help patients feel supported across time and not abandoned.
• Encouragement: You acknowledged the patient’s desire to maintain hope and gave basic advice (memory/brain exercises) when asked, showing willingness to problem-solve.

• Explicitness and Clarity (Medical Situation & Prognosis): You did not clearly state the diagnosis (glioblastoma), nor did you explain what it means in plain language. Avoiding jargon and providing a clear headline about the pathology findings are essential. Prognosis was not addressed at all.

• Structure and Standard of Care: The standard next steps after subtotal resection (consultation with neuro-oncology, chemo/radiation, seizure precautions, multidisciplinary care) were not discussed. Be specific about what happens next so the patient can plan and anticipate.

• Empathy & Validation: Opportunities for empathizing were missed repeatedly. When the patient shared fears and anxieties (about parenting, work), these were not validated (“That sounds overwhelming. Many people feel anxious at this point—you’re not alone.”). Emotional distress was not explicitly recognized or addressed.

• Communication and Comprehension Checks: The language used was often vague or unclear, and your responses drifted into cryptic comments (“Tell me more about the pathology was nice”, “Or you’re inserting the button”, etc.). This caused confusion, leaving the patient unclear and sometimes more anxious. Always check comprehension using “teach-back” — ask the patient to repeat in their own words what they understand.

• Empowering: While some open-ended questions were used, you missed opportunities to ask about the patient’s preferred level of information (e.g., “Would you like me to explain what the results mean and what comes next?”), to give space for questions, or to involve family in information sharing.
• Safety and Functionality: Safety planning regarding work, driving, and child care needs careful, explicit discussion, especially with brain tumor patients. This was not clearly addressed.

• MVP Protocol Integration: The conversation rarely addressed the full MVP framework: Medical Situation (diagnosis, prognosis, options), Values (what matters most to the patient), and Plan (clear next steps supported by practical resources). Integrate each step deliberately.

• State the Diagnosis and Prognosis Clearly: Use plain language, e.g., “Your results show a type of brain tumor called glioblastoma. This is a very serious cancer, but we have treatments we will discuss.”

• Map the Next Steps: Outline the usual next steps: referral to neuro-oncology, possible radiation and chemotherapy, seizure safety, and support services. Offer concrete supports (social work, care coordination).
• Validate and Empathize: When patients express fears or skepticism, acknowledge and normalize (“It’s hard to take all this in—many people feel overwhelmed”).
• Check for Understanding and Preferences: Ask, “Can you tell me what you understand so far?” and “How much information would you like today about what we know and what happens next?”
• Facilitate Patient Questions: Invite questions throughout: “What are your biggest worries that we haven’t discussed yet?”
• Summarize and Teach-Back: At the end, summarize the conversation: “Let me make sure we’re on the same page…”

Friendly Closing: The conversation shows your commitment to helping, but more structure, clarity, empathy, and practical support would greatly benefit your patients during these difficult discussions.
